panels.title: Components and signals of the plant

options.content:
SEDA-Lab simulates a **microgrid**: a small electrical network with its own sources of power, connected to the public grid. Its signals and their usual values come from a real microgrid at Mesa del Sol, in New Mexico (United States). That is why the frequency is 60 Hz, not 50 Hz as in Spain, and the voltage about 480 V: they are the values of the grid in the United States.

Four sources (the battery, the solar panels, the gas engine and the fuel cell) feed the **main bus**, to which the plant's equipment is connected. The **main circuit breaker** joins the main bus to the **grid connection point**, where the public grid arrives. A **cooling system** removes the heat that the fuel cell produces. The simulator publishes every signal every 5 seconds. It does not model the electrical physics: each signal is generated on its own, so a change in one does not move the others.

The signal names come from the real plant. MG-LV-MSB is the low-voltage main switchboard of the microgrid, that is, its main bus. MCCB is a type of circuit breaker. The breaker's signal is named after *island mode*: how a microgrid runs on its own sources when this breaker disconnects it from the grid. The table says what each signal measures in a real plant, where the signals do depend on each other.

| Component | Signal | What it measures in a real plant | Usual value in SEDA-Lab |
|---|---|---|---|
| Battery | `Battery_Active_Power` | Power that the battery delivers. Negative while it charges | −0.6 to 0.1 kW |
| PV power conversion system | `PVPCS_Active_Power` | Power from the solar (photovoltaic, PV) panels | about 0 kW at night, up to 39 kW at midday |
| Gas engine | `GE_Active_Power` | Power from an engine that burns gas to turn a generator. Slightly negative while it is stopped, when its own equipment draws a little power | about 54 kW at night, when it runs. About −1 kW by day, when it is stopped |
| Fuel cell | `FC_Active_Power` | Power from the fuel cell, which turns a fuel into electricity and heat | about 37 kW |
| Main circuit breaker | `Island_mode_MCCB_Active_Power` | Power that flows between the plant and the grid. Its sign gives the direction of the flow | −45 to −11 kW: always the same direction |
| Main bus | `MG-LV-MSB_AC_Voltage` | Voltage inside the plant. The same as the grid voltage while the plant is connected | about 484 V |
| Main bus | `MG-LV-MSB_Frequency` | Balance between power generated and power used. It falls if more power is used than generated | 60.00 Hz |
| Grid connection point | `Receiving_Point_AC_Voltage` | Voltage that the public grid delivers to the plant | about 484 V |
| Cooling system | `Inlet_Temperature_of_Chilled_Water` | Temperature of the water entering the cooling system | 18 to 24 °C |
| Cooling system | `Outlet_Temperature` | Temperature of the water leaving the cooling system | 18 to 23 °C |

The solar power, the gas engine and the two temperatures follow the simulator's day. Its daylight runs from 06:00 to 18:00 UTC (07:00 to 19:00 in Spain in winter), and the rest is night.

The gas engine runs mostly at night, when there is no solar power. Its power is drawn three ways on the right: each **last value** as it arrives every 5 seconds, its **average over the last minute**, and its **average over the last 15 minutes**.

The longer the period of the average, the smoother the line, and the later it shows a change. Compare the three lines: which one would show at once that the engine has stopped? Which would you use to compare one hour with the next?

panels.title: Gas engine power with its averages over 1 and 15 minutes

targets.rawSql: SELECT ts AS time, value AS "last value" FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 3 AND $__timeFilter(ts) ORDER BY 1

SELECT time, v AS "average over 1 minute" FROM (SELECT ts AS time, avg(value) OVER (ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN interval '1 minute' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS v FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 3 AND ts > $__timeFrom()::timestamp - interval '1 minute') s WHERE $__timeFilter(time) ORDER BY 1

SELECT time, v AS "average over 15 minutes" FROM (SELECT ts AS time, avg(value) OVER (ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN interval '15 minutes' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS v FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 3 AND ts > $__timeFrom()::timestamp - interval '15 minutes') s WHERE $__timeFilter(time) ORDER BY 1

panels.title: A value and how old it is

options.content:
The newest outlet temperature, and **how many seconds ago** it was measured. If the simulator or the data pipeline stops, the value stays on the screen unchanged, and only its age tells you that it is old. The age turns red above 30 s.

The table of the dashboard *Plant — as delivered* shows the time of each measurement instead, and leaves you to compare it with the clock.

targets.rawSql: SELECT value AS "°C" FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 10 ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1

panels.title: Age of the newest outlet temperature

targets.rawSql: SELECT round(extract(epoch FROM ((now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') - max(ts)))::numeric, 0) AS "age" FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 10 AND ts <= (now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')

options.content:
In SEDA-Lab the outlet temperature stays between **18 and 23 °C**, its normal range. The line is grey while the value is normal. Above **24 °C**, which it does not reach in normal operation, it turns orange: an early warning, before the alarm. Above **30 °C**, the threshold of Node-RED's alarm HIGH_OUTLET_TEMPERATURE, it turns red. The dashed lines mark 24 and 30 °C.

On a screen that is grey by default, a colour tells you at once that something is abnormal (ISA-101, the standard for operators' screens).

panels.title: Outlet temperature against its normal range

targets.rawSql: SELECT ts AS time, value AS "outlet °C" FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 10 AND $__timeFilter(ts) ORDER BY 1

options.content:
The value says where the temperature is. Its **trend**, the change over the last minute, says where it is going: 20 °C and steady is normal, but 20 °C and rising 3 °C a minute is not.

Each point compares a value with the one stored 12 measurements before it, which is one minute earlier when no measurement is missing. After a gap in the data, that earlier value is older, so the change can look large although the plant did not change.

targets.rawSql: SELECT ts AS time, value AS "°C" FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 10 AND $__timeFilter(ts) ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Change of the outlet temperature over 1 minute

targets.rawSql: SELECT time, d AS "°C per minute" FROM (SELECT ts AS time, value - lag(value, 12) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS d FROM measurement WHERE variable_id = 10 AND ts > $__timeFrom()::timestamp - interval '2 minutes') s WHERE $__timeFilter(time) ORDER BY 1

options.content:
The newest inlet and outlet temperatures of the cooling system, drawn as bars, gauges and a pie chart. From each of the three panels, try to tell which temperature is higher, and by how much.

People read a length on a common scale more accurately than an angle or an area (Cleveland and McGill, 1984), so the bars answer best and the pie chart worst.

targets.rawSql: SELECT v.code AS metric, m.value FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ON (variable_id) variable_id, value FROM measurement WHERE variable_id IN (9, 10) ORDER BY variable_id, ts DESC) m JOIN variable_catalog v ON v.id = m.variable_id

SELECT v.code AS metric, m.value FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ON (variable_id) variable_id, value FROM measurement WHERE variable_id IN (9, 10) ORDER BY variable_id, ts DESC) m JOIN variable_catalog v ON v.id = m.variable_id

panels.title: Cooling temperatures as a pie chart

targets.rawSql: SELECT v.code AS metric, m.value FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ON (variable_id) variable_id, value FROM measurement WHERE variable_id IN (9, 10) ORDER BY variable_id, ts DESC) m JOIN variable_catalog v ON v.id = m.variable_id

options.content:
Each point is the number of measurements stored in one minute, as a percentage of the **120** expected: 10 signals, each published 12 times a minute (every 5 seconds). The current minute is not drawn until it ends.

An indicator computed from these measurements, such as an average over a minute, is wrong when some are missing. A minute with no measurements has no point at all: look for a gap in the line, not for a zero.

targets.rawSql: SELECT date_trunc('minute', ts) AS time, round(count(*) * 100.0 / 120, 1) AS "completeness %" FROM measurement WHERE ts >= date_trunc('minute', $__timeFrom()::timestamp) AND ts < date_trunc('minute', (now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

options.content: The state of each Grafana alert rule: *Normal*, *Pending* (the condition holds, but not yet for long enough), *Firing* (it has held long enough) or *No Data* (no measurements arrive). Your group's rule appears here once you create it, later in this workshop.
